Curvature-aware Expected Free Energy as an Acquisition Function for
Bayesian Optimization*
Ajith Anil Meera1and Wouter Kouw2
Abstract— We propose an Expected Free Energy-based ac-
quisition function for Bayesian optimization to solve the joint
learning and optimization problem, i.e., optimize and learn
the underlying function simultaneously. We show that, under
specific assumptions, Expected Free Energy reduces to Upper
Confidence Bound, Lower Confidence Bound, and Expected
Information Gain. We prove that Expected Free Energy has
unbiased convergence guarantees for concave functions. Using
the results from these derivations, we introduce a curvature-
aware update law for Expected Free Energy and show its proof
of concept using a system identification problem on a Van der
Pol oscillator. Through rigorous simulation experiments, we
show that our adaptive Expected Free Energy-based acquisition
function outperforms state-of-the-art acquisition functions with
the least final simple regret and error in learning the Gaussian
process.
I. INTRODUCTION
Joint optimization and learning is central to robotics
and control, where an agent must acquire an accurate
map of the environment (or a phenomenon) and identify
high-value regions (e.g., areas of high human occupancy
in search-and-rescue or high detection likelihood in target
search). Fast and efficient information gathering can improve
productivity in precision agriculture, save lives in search
and rescue operations, and can aid industrial inspection and
maintenance [1]. Since real-world queries are costly, it is
crucial to develop methods that efficiently query at the fastest
rate for joint optimization and learning. However, most
acquisition functions (AFs) are designed to perform efficient
optimization and not to accurately learn the underlying
function [2]. We aim to bridge this gap by proposing an
acquisition function for Bayesian Optimization (BO), that
balances exploration and exploitation using the curvature
information, not just to optimize, but also to learn the
underlying function [3]. Taking inspiration from active in-
ference [4], the leading computational neuroscience theory
on how our brain performs inference, we propose Expected
Free Energy (EFE) as a new acquisition function. We point
towards EFE being a general acquisition function from which
other acquisition functions such as Upper Confidence Bound
(UCB) [5], Lower Confidence Bound (LCB) and Expected
Information Gain (EIG) can be derived.
BO has an extensive literature on AFs for black-box op-
timization [6], including information-theoretic regret bounds
[5]. Since BO is particularly useful for optimizing multi-
modal functions that are expensive to evaluate, it has seen

and for system identification [8]. The idea of using gradient
information to improve BO has also been extensively studied,
especially with regard to observed gradients [9], [10] and
posterior gradients [11]. Our method differs from these
approaches as we use the second gradient of the Gaussian
process (GP) posterior to adapt the balance between explo-
ration and exploitation. There has been a growing interest in
using the ideas from active inference for BO. Recent related
work proposed an active inference-based AF by placing a
Boltzmann distribution-based energy function on the prefer-
ence distribution [12]. Our work differs in that we start our
EFE derivation specifically from a Gaussian preference prior,
as a special case. This route is more elegant because a simple
linearization step directly recovers UCB and LCB, without
having to make unrealistic assumptions [12]. We further
improve on this EFE by proposing a curvature-aware rule
to improve the performance. Another similar work is [13],
which proposed an active inference-based AF. They used
the free energy of the expected future [14] as the objective,
instead of EFE, which is fundamentally different from our
formulation, and missed out on uncovering the equivalence
between UCB and active inference. The core novelty of
our work is the use of curvature information within the
EFE acquisition function to balance between exploration and
exploitation for a joint optimization and learning problem.
We mathematically show that the stationary point of EFE
is curvature agnostic. Based on this result, we propose a
novel curvature-aware adaptive rule for EFE that encourages
resampling in high curvature regions and exploring uncertain
regions with low curvature. The core contributions of this
paper include: i) a proof that, under specific assumptions,
EFE reduces to UCB, LCB and EIG (Sec. III-B), ii) a
proof for EFE’s unbiased convergence on concave functions
(Sec. IV-A), iii) introduction of a curvature-aware update
rule for EFE (Sec. IV-B), and iv) showing that our adaptive
(curvature-aware) EFE outperforms state-of-the-art AFs for
joint optimization and learning (Sec. V).

III. EFE AND OTHER ACQUISITION FUNCTIONS
This section derives EFE for a GP and shows that UCB
and LCB are linear surrogates of EFE.
A. EFE under a GP Model

problem in which an agent must learn from interactions
with its environment to reach a goal. Exploration refers to
learning the function (discovering its shape), and exploitation

represented by the value of the unknown function at that
query location. We implicitly assume that the environment

action that optimally balances exploration and exploitation

B. Curvature-aware EFE via adaptiveτ2
Resampling around high curvature regions provides two
advantages, one for optimization and the other for learning:
i) discovering and refining a potential optimal solution and
ii) a better GP learning around all local optima. However,
exploring low curvature regions with high uncertainty is also
vital. Therefore, we need an algorithm that can combine
the information about curvature and uncertainty to adapt its
degree of exploration and exploitation. An effective strategy
for efficient joint optimization and learning of multi-modal
functions would be to balance between exploration and
exploitation by i) jumping into the local optima of high
curvature regions with low uncertainty and ii) exploring low
curvature regions with high uncertainty. Taking inspiration
from Theorem IV .1, we define a novel update rule forτ2to

This update rule automatically shifts the EFE in (5) between
exploration and exploitation by responding to the local
curvature and uncertainty of the GP. When the posterior

the update makesτ2small, pushing EFE toward exploitation

In this way, the update law continuously balances the two
behaviors, exploiting structure where the model is confident
and exploring where it lacks information. This endows EFE
with an inherent preference for resampling around high
curvature regions where a potential optimum could be found.
V. SIMULATION EXPERIMENTS
This section aims to show the superior performance of our
adaptive EFE over state-of-the-art AFs on a joint learning and
optimization problem. We show the proof of concept of our
adaptive EFE on a simple system identification problem and
then generalize the result on a highly randomized function
space against six other benchmarks.

A. Adaptive and non-adaptive EFE
This section shows the advantage of our adaptive EFE over
non-adaptive EFE using a system identification problem on
a Van der Pol oscillator given by:
¨x−κ(1−x2) ˙x+x= 0,
whereκmust be inferred. The reference trajectory is gen-
erated with the true valueκ= 3from the initial condition
x(0) = 0.5,˙x(0) = 0with noiseσ n= 0.1and sampling
time∆t= 0.05s. As the initial segment is dominated by
transient dynamics and is weakly informative for parameter
estimation, the objective is evaluated only on the steady–state
windowt∈[20,60]. We take the negative mean-squared
error (MSE) between the simulated trajectory at a candidate
parameterκand the noisy observed reference as the BO
objective. Figure 1 shows the results of BO using adaptive
and nonadaptive EFE (50 iterations each), overlayed on the
true function. Although both of them successfully found the
optimum parameter atκ= 3, adaptive EFE has learned the
underlying cost function more accurately by exploring all
regions of high curvature. Nonadaptive EFE on the other
hand skipped the low-valued high curvature regions. This
demonstrates the superior performance of our adaptive EFE
for joint optimization and learning.
Fig. 1. While both methods find the correct parameterκ= 3(repeated
samples around the maximum), adaptive EFE (top) results in a better joint
optimization and learning by exploring all high curvature regions. The non
adaptive EFE (bottom) on the other hand, neglects high curvature regions.
B. Learning and Optimization
To assess the performance of adaptive EFE across di-
verse landscapes, we benchmark all AFs on a collection of
randomly generated one-dimensional objectives constructed
from10sinusoidal and cosinusoidal components with ran-
dom amplitudes, frequencies and phases. Each objective is
defined on[−8,8]and evaluated on a fixed grid of400
points. Across50independent objectives, all BO methods
start from the same three initial design points and are run for
50iterations under identical observation noise (σ n= 0.2).
Details of simulation settings are given in Appendix D.
Performance is reported using the final GP regression error
(MSE over the domain) and the simple regret relative tothe true global maximum, enabling a fair comparison of
average performance and variability over heterogeneous test
functions. Figure 2 shows the results comparing adaptive
EFE with benchmarks UCB, Expected Improvement (EI),
Probability of Improvement (PI), V AR (σas the objective),
Thompson Sampling (TS) and Knowledge Gradient (KG).
Since EFE populates itself in the left-bottom region of the
plot, it is the best method for joint optimization and learning.
Table II reports the mean of all methods for the final MSE
and for the final simple regret. EFE has the lowest simple
regret and has a GP MSE that is close to the pure exploration
strategy (V AR). This shows that in a highly randomized
general 1D function space, EFE outperforms other AFs for
the joint optimization and learning problem.

VI. CONCLUSIONS
EFE has a strong potential as a next-generation BO
acquisition as it unifies exploration and exploitation in a
principled way. Taking inspiration from this, we introduced
a novel curvature-aware EFE acquisition function for BO
for the joint learning and optimization problem. We mathe-
matically showed that UCB and LCB are linear surrogates
of EFE, and that EFE has unbiased convergence guarantees
for concave functions. Our simulation results show that EFE
is very competitive in comparison with state-of-the-art AFs.

A natural direction for future work is to develop scalable,
MPC-style multi-step EFE planners that propagate GP be-
liefs along candidate action sequences, enabling non-myopic
query selection that anticipates the full evolution of future
posterior states. Such planners could substantially improve
the efficiency of information gathering, enabling agents to
efficiently perform real-world exploration, monitoring, and
decision-making tasks.

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary:
This partial document introduces a novel acquisition function called Curvature-aware Expected Free Energy (EFE) for Bayesian Optimization (BO). The primary goal is to address the joint learning and optimization problem, where the system simultaneously learns an underlying function and optimizes it.

Key points covered include:

*   **EFE as a General Acquisition Function:** The document proposes EFE as a new acquisition function inspired by active inference. It demonstrates that under certain assumptions, EFE can reduce to well-known acquisition functions like Upper Confidence Bound (UCB), Lower Confidence Bound (LCB), and Expected Information Gain (EIG).
*   **Theoretical Guarantees:** The paper provides a proof that EFE has unbiased convergence guarantees for concave functions.
*   **Curvature-Aware Update Law:** A novel curvature-aware update rule for EFE is introduced. This rule aims to improve performance by considering the curvature of the function, encouraging resampling in high-curvature regions and exploration in low-curvature, uncertain regions.
*   **Empirical Validation:** The effectiveness of the proposed curvature-aware EFE is demonstrated through simulation experiments on a system identification problem (Van der Pol oscillator). The results show that this adaptive EFE outperforms state-of-the-art acquisition functions in terms of final simple regret and accuracy in learning the Gaussian process model.
*   **Distinction from Prior Work:** The document highlights how their approach differs from existing methods, particularly in its use of the second gradient of the Gaussian process posterior and its derivation of EFE from a Gaussian preference prior, which allows for a more direct recovery of UCB and LCB.

structure.title: PROBLEM STATEMENT
structure.summary:
This document introduces a novel acquisition function for Bayesian Optimization called Curvature-aware Expected Free Energy (EFE). The primary goal is to address the joint learning and optimization problem, where the system simultaneously learns an underlying function and optimizes it.

The main points covered are:

It demonstrates that under specific assumptions, EFE can reduce to well-known acquisition functions like Upper Confidence Bound (UCB), Lower Confidence Bound (LCB), and Expected Information Gain (EIG).
*   **Theoretical Guarantees:** The document provides a proof that EFE has unbiased convergence guarantees for concave functions.
*   **Curvature-Aware Update Law:** A key contribution is the introduction of a curvature-aware update rule for EFE. This rule leverages the second gradient of the Gaussian Process (GP) posterior to adapt the balance between exploration and exploitation, encouraging resampling in high curvature regions and exploration in low curvature regions.
*   **Empirical Validation:** The proposed curvature-aware EFE is validated on a system identification problem involving a Van der Pol oscillator. Simulation experiments show that this adaptive EFE outperforms state-of-the-art acquisition functions in terms of final simple regret and accuracy in learning the Gaussian Process.
*   **Problem Formulation:** The document formally defines the problem of joint learning and optimization within the context of Bayesian Optimization using a Gaussian Process model.
*   **Derivation of EFE:** A detailed derivation of the EFE for a GP model is presented, breaking it down into pragmatic (exploitation) and epistemic (exploration) value terms. The role of a parameter ($\tau^{-2}$) in balancing these terms is highlighted.
*   **Relationship to Existing Methods:** The paper contrasts its approach with existing methods, particularly those using gradient information or active inference, emphasizing the novelty of using curvature information within the EFE framework and its direct derivation of UCB/LCB without unrealistic assumptions.

structure.title: EFE AND OTHER ACQUISITION FUNCTIONS:
structure.summary:
The partial document discusses the concept of Expected Functional Gain (EFE) in the context of optimizing an unknown function using a Gaussian Process (GP) model. It frames this as an active inference problem where an agent learns from interactions to balance exploration (learning the function's shape) and exploitation (optimizing the function's value).

The main points covered are:

*   **Problem Formulation:** Joint learning and optimization involves sequentially choosing query locations to improve the GP's mean prediction and maximize the function's value.
*   **EFE Definition:** EFE is defined as a functional that balances "pragmatic value" (expected deviation from preferred observations) and "epistemic value" (expected reduction in uncertainty about the latent function).
*   **EFE under GP Model:** The document derives a one-step ahead (myopic) EFE for a GP, assuming a Gaussian preference over outcomes.
*   **Approximation:** A key assumption is made to approximate the full GP information gain by considering only the marginal information gain at the queried location.
*   **EFE Components:** The derived EFE is shown to consist of terms that penalize deviations from preferred outcomes and large predictive uncertainty (pragmatic value), and a term that rewards informative measurements by reducing latent uncertainty (epistemic value).
*   **Balancing Exploration and Exploitation:** The parameter $\tau^{-2}$ in the EFE formulation is identified as a mechanism to control the balance between exploration and exploitation.
*   **Relation to Other Acquisition Functions:** The document demonstrates that EFE is a generalization of other Bayesian Optimization acquisition functions, specifically showing how Lower Confidence Bound (LCB) can be derived from EFE under certain restrictions.

nodes.title: Relations to known acquisitions:
nodes.summary:
The provided document excerpt focuses on the concept of Expected Functional Entropy (EFE) as an acquisition function for Bayesian optimization, particularly in the context of optimizing an unknown function represented by a Gaussian Process (GP).

The main points covered are:

*   **Problem Formulation:** The problem is framed as jointly learning an unknown function and optimizing it by sequentially choosing query locations. This involves balancing exploration (learning the function's shape) and exploitation (finding the maximum value).
*   **EFE Definition:** EFE is defined as a functional that balances "pragmatic value" (expected deviation from preferred observations) and "epistemic value" (expected reduction in uncertainty about the latent function).
*   **EFE under GP Model:** The document derives the EFE for a GP, breaking it down into its pragmatic and epistemic components. It introduces a preference for observations around a target value ($y^*$) and a Gaussian noise model.
*   **Assumption 1 (Marginal Information Gain):** A key assumption is made to simplify the EFE calculation by considering only the marginal information gain at the queried location, rather than the full GP information gain.
*   **EFE Components and Balancing Exploration/Exploitation:** The pragmatic term is shown to penalize deviations from preferred outcomes and large predictive uncertainty, while the epistemic term rewards informative measurements by reducing latent uncertainty. The parameter $\tau^{-2}$ is identified as a crucial factor for balancing exploration and exploitation.
*   **Relationship to Known Acquisition Functions:** The document demonstrates how EFE generalizes and reduces to other well-known acquisition functions:
    *   **Lower Confidence Bound (LCB):** Derived by considering only the pragmatic value of EFE and linearizing it.
    *   **Upper Confidence Bound (UCB):** Derived by linearizing the full EFE under specific regimes.
    *   **Expected Information Gain (EIG):** Shown to be equivalent to the epistemic term of EFE under Assumption 1.
*   **EFE as a General Acquisition Function:** The authors hypothesize that the full form of EFE is a more general acquisition function with potentially superior performance, especially when considering correlations between function values at different locations.
*   **Convergence Analysis (Brief Mention):** Section IV briefly introduces the convergence analysis of EFE-based acquisition functions, mentioning a sufficient condition for unbiased local convergence and a curvature-aware update rule.

structure.title: UNBIASED CONVERGENCE AND CURVATURE-AWARE EFE:
structure.summary:
The provided document excerpt focuses on the theoretical underpinnings and practical implications of an acquisition function called EFE (Expected Feature Exploration). It establishes relationships between EFE and other common acquisition functions like UCB (Upper Confidence Bound) and LCB (Lower Confidence Bound) by analyzing their behavior under specific assumptions and through local linearization.

Key points covered include:

*   **LCB as a Linear Surrogate of EFE:** The document shows that under certain conditions (specifically, when the pragmatic value dominates the epistemic value and the posterior uncertainty is high), LCB can be viewed as a first-order approximation of EFE, aiming to maximize the mean while penalizing uncertainty.
*   **UCB as a Local Linearization of EFE:** Similarly, UCB is presented as a local linear approximation of the full EFE. Under different regimes (where the mean is much smaller than the target and noise variance is low compared to the model variance), minimizing EFE is shown to be equivalent to maximizing a UCB-like expression.
*   **EFE's Epistemic Term Equals EIG:** A significant finding is that the epistemic (information gain) component of EFE, when the pragmatic term is dropped, is mathematically equivalent to the Expected Information Gain (EIG).
*   **EFE as a General Acquisition Function:** The authors hypothesize that EFE, in its full form, is a more general acquisition function that encompasses UCB, LCB, and EIG as special cases under different simplifications or assumptions. This generality is suggested to lead to superior performance, especially when considering correlations in data.
*   **Convergence Analysis of EFE:** The document provides a theoretical condition for the unbiased local convergence of EFE. It demonstrates that a specific relationship between the model variance, noise variance, and a parameter $\tau^2$ is sufficient for EFE to converge to the true optimum in a local neighborhood.
*   **Curvature-Aware EFE via Adaptive $\tau^2$:** Based on the convergence analysis, a novel adaptive update rule for $\tau^2$ is proposed. This rule dynamically adjusts $\tau^2$ based on the local curvature and uncertainty of the Gaussian Process model. The goal is to balance exploration (in flat, uncertain regions) and exploitation (in sharply curved regions with low uncertainty), leading to more efficient joint learning and optimization.
*   **Simulation Experiments:** The document outlines plans for simulation experiments to demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed adaptive EFE against existing state-of-the-art acquisition functions on system identification and general function optimization problems.

nodes.title: Unbiased convergence guarantees for concave functions:
nodes.summary:
The provided document excerpt focuses on the theoretical underpinnings and practical implementation of an "Expected Feasible Improvement" (EFE) acquisition function, particularly in the context of Bayesian optimization.

The main points covered are:

*   **Unbiased Local Convergence of EFE:** The document proves that a specific condition on the parameter $\tau^2$ (namely, $\tau^2 = \sigma^2(x^\star) + \sigma_n^2$) is sufficient for the EFE to converge to the true optimum ($x^\star$) locally and without bias. This condition ensures that the maximizer of the EFE in a small neighborhood of $x^\star$ is indeed $x^\star$.
*   **Mathematical Derivation:** A detailed mathematical derivation is presented, using second-order Taylor expansions of the Gaussian Process (GP) mean ($\mu(x)$) and variance ($\sigma^2(x)$) around the optimum $x^\star$. This derivation leads to a quadratic approximation of the EFE and the calculation of its stationary point.
*   **Conditions for Unbiasedness and Local Maximality:** The derivation explicitly shows how the condition $\tau^2 = \sigma^2(x^\star) + \sigma_n^2$ leads to an unbiased stationary point ($h_{EFE} = 0$) and a local maximum for the EFE.
*   **Limitations of Standard EFE:** Two key observations are highlighted: the stationary point of the EFE is independent of the curvature of the underlying function, and the optimal $\tau^2$ depends on an unknown term $\sigma^2(x^\star)$, making the standard EFE's stationary point "curvature agnostic."
*   **Curvature-Aware EFE via Adaptive $\tau^2$:** Inspired by the limitations, a novel approach is proposed to make the EFE "curvature-aware" by adaptively updating $\tau^2$.
*   **Proposed Update Rule for $\tau^2$:** A new update rule for $\tau^2$ is introduced: $\tau^{-2}_i = |\mu''(x)| + \sigma^2(x)$. This rule aims to balance exploration and exploitation by considering both the local curvature (second derivative of the mean) and the predictive uncertainty (variance).
*   **Tuning and Normalization of $\tau^2$:** The adaptive $\tau^2$ is then normalized and rescaled to a tunable range $[\tau^2_{min}, \tau^2_{max}]$ to represent pure exploitation and exploration strategies, respectively.
*   **Mechanism of Adaptive $\tau^2$:** The document explains how this adaptive rule influences the EFE. Small $\tau^2$ (in high curvature, low uncertainty regions) promotes exploitation, while large $\tau^2$ (in low curvature, high uncertainty regions) encourages exploration.
*   **Simulation Experiments:** The final section outlines the intention to demonstrate the superior performance of this adaptive EFE over state-of-the-art acquisition functions through simulation experiments, starting with a system identification problem and generalizing to a randomized function space.

structure.title: SIMULATION EXPERIMENTS:
structure.summary:
The provided document excerpt focuses on a novel acquisition function called "EFE" (Expected Feasible Region) for Bayesian Optimization (BO), particularly for joint optimization and learning problems.

The main points covered are:

*   **Theoretical Foundation of EFE:** The document presents a mathematical proof demonstrating that a specific condition on the parameter $\tau^2$ (related to the noise variance) ensures unbiased local convergence of EFE to the optimum. This condition is $\tau^2 = \sigma^2(x^\star) + \sigma_n^2$, where $\sigma^2(x^\star)$ is the variance at the optimum and $\sigma_n^2$ is the observation noise.
*   **Limitations of Non-Adaptive EFE:** The analysis reveals that the stationary point of the standard EFE is independent of the function's curvature. This implies that a non-adaptive EFE might miss important regions of high curvature where optima could lie.
*   **Introduction of Curvature-Aware EFE:** To address the limitations, a new "curvature-aware" EFE is proposed. This adaptive version modifies $\tau^2$ based on both the local curvature (second derivative of the mean prediction) and the predictive variance of the Gaussian Process (GP).
*   **Adaptive $\tau^2$ Update Rule:** The core of the adaptive EFE is the update rule for $\tau^2$, which aims to balance exploration and exploitation. It is designed to:
    *   Favor exploitation (smaller $\tau^2$) in regions of high curvature and low uncertainty.
    *   Favor exploration (larger $\tau^2$) in regions of low curvature and high uncertainty.
    *   This is achieved by making $\tau^2$ inversely proportional to the sum of the absolute curvature and the predictive variance.
*   **Simulation Experiments:** The document details simulation experiments to validate the performance of the adaptive EFE.
    *   **System Identification:** A Van der Pol oscillator system is used to compare adaptive EFE with non-adaptive EFE. The results show that adaptive EFE learns the underlying cost function more accurately by exploring high-curvature regions, while non-adaptive EFE skips them.
    *   **General Function Space:** The adaptive EFE is benchmarked against several state-of-the-art acquisition functions (UCB, EI, PI, VAR, TS, KG) on a collection of randomly generated 1D functions. The results indicate that EFE outperforms other methods in jointly optimizing and learning, achieving the lowest simple regret and a competitive GP Mean Squared Error (MSE).
*   **Conclusion:** The EFE acquisition function is presented as a promising next-generation BO tool that unifies exploration and exploitation. The proposed curvature-aware adaptation further enhances its performance for joint learning and optimization problems.

nodes.title: Adaptive and non-adaptive EFE:
nodes.summary:
The document discusses the advantages of an adaptive Expected Feasible Region (EFE) acquisition function for Bayesian Optimization (BO), particularly for problems involving joint optimization and learning.

Section A demonstrates the superiority of adaptive EFE over non-adaptive EFE using a system identification problem on a Van der Pol oscillator. The adaptive EFE is shown to learn the underlying cost function more accurately by exploring regions of high curvature, leading to better optimization results.

Section B further evaluates adaptive EFE against other acquisition functions (UCB, EI, PI, VAR, TS, KG) on a collection of randomly generated one-dimensional objective functions. The conclusions emphasize EFE's potential as a next-generation BO acquisition function due to its unified approach to exploration and exploitation. The introduction of a novel curvature-aware EFE is highlighted, along with mathematical proofs showing its relationship to UCB and LCB and its convergence guarantees. Simulation results confirm EFE's competitiveness against state-of-the-art acquisition functions.
